textRun.content: Digital Transformation of the RFQ Process in Commercial Pump Distribution — INSEAD EMBA Final Project
Problem in one sentence, with the three measured baseline numbers (time, cost, error rate).

The proposed solution in one sentence, plus the headline feasibility finding (“a structured audit of 30 historical RFQs found X% of extraction fields technically automatable with current document-AI capability; a calibrated process simulation projects median cycle time falling from X days to Y hours”) — evidence-led, but honestly ex-ante.

Financial headline as a range, not a point: projected NPV (P10 / P50 / P90 from the Monte Carlo in 9.5), payback, and the floor case (“clears the hurdle rate on cost savings alone under conservative assumptions”).
The strategic claim: transaction data as the distributor’s future moat.
The actual recommendation — and this framing is critical: not “build the system” but
“approve a stage-gated pilot investment of € X, with explicit go/no-go criteria at each gate.”
An ex-ante paper that recommends a bounded, testable next step is far more credible than one that recommends a rollout.

The RFQ from Innovo Contracting for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi lands at M.A.H.Y. Khoory's Abu Dhabi branch on a Thursday evening around 16:30: roughly 75 pumps across five applications, from booster sets to chilled water, with the quote due the following Tuesday. Khoory is competing against Grundfos, Xylem, Wilo and Lowara — and against at least one other distributor quoting the same Grundfos range it carries — so the job will be won or lost on price and speed of response as much as on brand.

Worked properly — every schedule and specification read, head losses calculated for each application, every selection run through the manufacturer software — an inquiry this size is close to twenty-eight hours of estimating work, and the branch has two estimators. Line managers bring both in over the weekend on overtime and borrow a third from another desk. It is not enough. Tuesday comes and the quotation is not ready.

The quote goes out two days late, seven calendar days after receipt. Innovo's senior management escalates to Khoory's leadership, and a face-to-face meeting is needed to settle the relationship. Khoory ultimately wins the project — but not on the strength of this quotation, and the paper returns to what that near-failure cost and why it keeps happening.

A distributor exists in this chain because the manufacturer cannot do what the distributor does — not economically, often not at all — and the first and costliest of its functions is technical expertise. Every RFQ means reading consultant specifications, CAD files and drawings, extracting flow, head and efficiency requirements, running head-loss calculations, and working out which model across a manufacturer's full range actually fits the site; for unusual applications it means going back to the manufacturer for a special quote before pricing the contractor. A multinational manufacturer selling into dozens of regions cannot build that regional depth itself. It is exactly this function that nearly failed under pressure in the Innovo inquiry.

The second function is credit: rather than extend project-linked payment terms, bank guarantees and retentions to dozens of individual contractors, the manufacturer works through one distributor and lets it carry the market and the credit risk.
The third is local presence — testing, commissioning and warranty support from a party the contractor can actually reach when something goes wrong.

Each of these functions is under pressure from digitization, and this paper examines what happens when the most defensible of them becomes automatable. Credit and local presence are largely fixed costs of being in the market; technical expertise is not — it needs trained estimators and hours of manual work per inquiry, and it scales directly with volume and complexity. The question the paper pursues is whether the reading, the calculations and the model selection can be digitized without losing the judgment that makes them valuable.

A standard inquiry — three to twelve pumps across one or two applications — takes an estimator around five and a half hours of concentrated work: reading the specification and CAD files, running head loss calculations, selecting the model, and pricing it. The largest inquiries — several dozen pumps across multiple applications; the Innovo package ran to seventy-five — demand twenty-five to thirty hours of estimating effort and require pulling multiple estimators simultaneously, against deadlines sometimes as tight as two to three days. These large inquiries arrive roughly once a month but cannot be staffed as if routine. Timing costs real business: an estimated 15% of tenders are lost specifically to late or rushed quotes (E, sales and management interviews; treated as an upper bound and triangulated in 9.3) — concentrated among first-time customers with no relationship to buy patience, and fast-track projects landing while the team is already stretched.

Khoory carries 16 estimators across all branches, each handling roughly 12 RFQs a week across the company's full product range. A fully loaded estimator costs the business approximately €22,000 a year. Hiring a qualified replacement takes two to three months, and a further three to four months before they are fully productive. Estimator capacity is therefore a hard constraint rather than a soft one: it directly determines how fast the business can take on new sales and new customers, independent of demand.

Errors are not rare. Across the 2025 quotation audit, roughly one standard inquiry in nine went out containing at least one defect — a wrong model, a wrong price, or a missed specification requirement — rising to one in five on the largest, most valuable work. The full error taxonomy and its cost consequences are developed in Section 4.4.
What process architecture could automate the RFQ process while preserving quote quality, and what evidence supports its technical feasibility?
What is the projected financial impact of the proposed transformation, and how robust is that projection under uncertainty?
What are the strategic implications for the distributor’s position in the value chain, and what implementation path best manages the risks?

Slow turnaround, hard capacity constraints and error rates that erode margin and trust are all downstream of one question: whether the distributor's technical-expertise function can be automated without losing the judgment that makes it valuable. Three research questions address it — RQ1 in Sections 6 through 8, RQ2 in Section 9, RQ3 in Sections 10 and 11.

The scope is limited to pumps, where the technical selection burden is heaviest and the case for automation strongest; valves, HVAC and Khoory's other product lines are excluded, though they are the natural extension once the pump-focused system is proven.
The UAE only, where the volume and the pain are concentrated today; GCC expansion is a near-term next step, since specifications and practices across the region closely mirror the UAE market.

The technical workflow from RFQ receipt through quote generation, plus the submittal stage once a project is won. The commercial negotiation between quote and LOI is excluded deliberately: the paper automates the distributor's technical-judgment function, not its deal-making.

This is an ex-ante study: no software has been built and no pilot run. The analysis rests on a calibrated simulation of the current process, an audited feasibility assessment, and a financial projection under uncertainty (Sections 6–9); a live pilot is recommended, not conducted (Section 11).
Section 3 — Methodology: An Ex-Ante Evaluation Design

This study is a prospective — ex-ante — evaluation of a proposed process transformation. Nothing described in Sections 6 through 8 has been built, and the paper claims otherwise nowhere. Its claim is narrower: that the transformation can be evaluated to a decision-grade standard before a line of code exists, with the discipline applied to any capital investment — measure the current state, design the alternative from established components, model its behaviour, and subject the assumptions to structured challenge.
Four components carry the evaluation: an
of the current quoting process, measured rather than recalled (Section 4); a
assembled from components whose individual behaviour is documented, so that the novelty lies in the assembly rather than in any unproven part (Section 7); a
— a process model for cycle time and capacity, and a financial model that converts its outputs into a probabilistic investment case (Sections 8 and 9); and
, in which the estimators and contractors are used not as sources of enthusiasm but as adversaries of the design's assumptions (8.1, 8.3, 4.6).

One scoping statement belongs here because every number downstream depends on it. Khoory operates 16 estimators across its UAE branches, each handling on the order of twelve inquiries a week across all the product lines the company distributes. The empirical baseline of Section 4 was measured at a single branch — [the Abu Dhabi estimation office] — whose 640 pump RFQs in 2025 constitute the study population, the slice of that workload within this paper's product scope; company-wide figures appear only where Section 9 scales the branch-level findings, and are labelled as such when they do. Measuring one branch deeply was preferred to measuring all branches thinly: the simulation of Section 8 needs step-level timings that only observation can supply, and observation does not spread.
Every quantitative claim in the paper carries one of three tags, used without exception.
means read directly from records or timestamped observation.
means produced by the structured feasibility study of 8.1, scored by estimators against a written rubric on real historical documents.

means an output of the process or financial model, traceable to a named assumption in Appendix A. The vocabulary is the paper's contract with its reader: at any sentence, it should be unambiguous which kind of knowledge is being offered.

Table 3.1 lists every source of evidence the paper draws on, what each supplies, and the section where it does its work. No other data enters the analysis. All monetary figures in this paper are stated in euros, converted from UAE dirhams at AED 1 = €0.23; the underlying records are dirham-denominated.

Two models do the projective work of this paper, and one rule governs both: a model earns the right to project a future it has not seen only by first reproducing a past that was measured.

represents the branch operation as a flow of inquiries through the steps of Exhibit 4.1 — arrivals by tier at measured 2025 rates, touch times from the observed step distributions, estimator capacity as the constraint, queue discipline as observed, with large inquiries modelled as pre-emption because that is what the Innovo case shows happens. It runs on the authors' operations-simulation platform (5.5). Before any to-be scenario is run, the model must reproduce the measured as-is baseline — median and P90 cycle time by tier, within a stated tolerance — and the calibration error is reported in 8.2, because it is the number that separates simulation from arithmetic. Only then are to-be scenarios run across the audited automation range, reporting cycle time, utilization and capacity as distributions.

converts those projections into an investment case by Monte Carlo, because the honest state of knowledge in an ex-ante study is a set of ranges. Three uncertain inputs are treated as distributions — the automation rate (bounded by the 8.1 audit), the win-rate uplift from faster quoting (triangulated in 9.3 and floored at zero in the conservative case), and the build cost (9.4) — producing five-year NPV at P10, P50 and P90 with the probability of clearing the hurdle rate. Every input distribution is documented in Appendix C; no parameter enters the model that the Appendix A register does not name.

Three limitations are acknowledged now and treated fully in Section 12. The baseline is one branch of one distributor, measured over one year, and the deep-observation sample behind the step timings is 22 inquiries. The future state is simulated and audited, not observed: no live extraction accuracy, engineer adoption, or contractor behaviour has been measured, and the pilot recommended in Section 11 exists precisely to supply what this design cannot. And the demand-side evidence — how much speed is worth in won tenders — rests on triangulated history and stated preferences rather than experiment, which is why the financial model floors that benefit at zero before it claims anything else.

Three sources anchor this section: the 2025 inquiry log (640 pump RFQs, M); three weeks of direct observation, during which 22 inquiries were timestamped from arrival to quotation (M); and the finance ledger of credit notes and rework traceable to quotation defects (M). Figures that could not be read directly from records were estimated from sampled data or structured interviews and are tagged (E). Everything the later sections project is anchored to what this section can demonstrate.
4.1 The as-is process: a swimlane view

An inquiry arrives as an email carrying some combination of a specification extract, a pump schedule — often a scanned image — a riser diagram, and occasionally a CAD file. From there it passes through nine steps and five roles before a quotation goes back out. Exhibit 4.1 maps the path, annotating each step with touch time (someone actively working on the inquiry) and queue time (the inquiry waiting its turn).

Exhibit 4.1. Median values across the 22 observed inquiries (M). The clarification loop and the management approval loop occur on a subset of inquiries; their queue times are medians within that subset.

The exhibit carries the central finding of the current-state study: the median case consumed 5.5 hours of actual work spread over roughly 39 working hours of elapsed time (M). Six hours out of every seven, nobody was working on the inquiry at all — it was waiting to be assigned, waiting in an estimator's personal queue, waiting on the contractor's answer, waiting for a discount approval. The work is not slow; the waiting is.
Exhibit 4.2. Touch and queue medians by inquiry tier (tiers defined in 4.2). The queue share is remarkably stable — between 86% and 88% — regardless of complexity (M).

Three steps account for most of the queueing: assignment (a median 14 working hours before an estimator picks the inquiry up), the clarification loop (a median 41 working hours for the contractor's answer, during which the process cannot move), and pricing approval. Each is a handover between people, and each handover is a queue. The cost side is simpler: at a fully loaded €12 per hour — €22,000 a year over roughly 1,840 productive hours (E, payroll records) — the median inquiry carries about €66 of direct labour, developed by tier in 4.3.

A single replacement circulator and a three-building museum package have nothing in common except the mailbox they arrive in, so every 2025 inquiry was classified retrospectively into three tiers by pump count, data completeness at receipt, and project value. Two staff members classified independently, agreeing on 91% of inquiries (E). The taxonomy carries through the paper: Section 7 routes by it, Section 8 samples by it, and Section 9 builds its benefits by it.
Chilled water, multi-building, special quotes to manufacturer
Table 4.1. Segmentation criteria and 2025 mix. n = 640 inquiries.

The inversion in the last two rows matters: Tier 3 supplies one inquiry in eight but nearly half the quoted value, so the commercially decisive inquiries are exactly where the process is slowest, the documents messiest, and the expertise thinnest — two estimators can handle a chilled-water package unassisted, and one of them handles most. A redesign that only worked for simple inquiries would automate the 12% of value that least needs help.
Table 4.2 consolidates the baseline. Every subsequent claim of improvement in this paper is a claim against one of these cells.

Table 4.2. Baseline metrics by tier, 2025. Cost per quote combines touch hours at loaded rates with a per-inquiry allocation of estimation software licences; defect rates were estimated by auditing a stratified sample of 120 quotations against source documents.

Three readings follow. First, cycle time grows faster than touch time as complexity rises — an 88-hour Tier 3 median contains only 11.4 hours of work — so the delay problem is structural, not a matter of effort. Second, the defect rate triples between Tier 1 and Tier 3, tracking the volume of manual transcription each tier demands. Third, and read together with the value shares in Table 4.1: the business earns its margin where its process performs worst. That tension is what the Innovo inquiry in 4.5 makes concrete.
4.4 Error taxonomy and the cost of poor quality

The audit of 120 sampled quotations, cross-checked against the credit-note ledger, surfaced four distinct classes of error. They differ not only in frequency but in when they are discovered, and discovery timing drives cost far more than the mistake itself: an extraction error caught at internal review costs an hour of rework, while the same error caught at commissioning costs a return shipment, a site visit, and a measure of trust.
Flow, head or model data mis-read or re-keyed wrongly from PDF, scan or drawing
Head-loss worked from wrong pipe length, material or fitting count; sizing off as a result
Feasible but wrong model — duty point at curve edge, wrong configuration for the application
Wrong list price, missed cost update, arithmetic in the discount line
Table 4.3. Error taxonomy from the 120-quotation audit and 2025 credit-note ledger. Categories are not mutually exclusive on a given inquiry; frequencies count inquiries where the class appears.

Summed across the year, the traceable cost of the four classes comes to roughly 1.2% of revenue (E). The chain matters as much as the total: nearly every calculation and selection error began life as an extraction problem, so attacking the point of entry starves much of the downstream taxonomy.

The larger leak never appears in an error report, because each instance looks like a reasonable commercial decision. Discounts are set case by case with no reference point in front of the pricer: matched 2025 quotations show discounts on comparable Tier 2 work ranging from 4% to 18% (M) — not because the jobs differed, but because the days did. Against the median like-for-like discount, the foregone margin is roughly 1.9% of revenue annually (E), half again as large as all four error classes combined, and invisible precisely because no single decision was wrong. Together, quality cost and discount leakage run to about 3.1% of revenue — the figure the pricing engine of Section 7.6 is designed against.
4.5 The Innovo inquiry: Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, as-is

The numbers above describe the process in aggregate; the Innovo inquiry that opened this paper shows what they feel like from inside. By the criteria of 4.2 it was a large Tier 3 inquiry — a specification extract running to dozens of pages, schedules scanned as images, riser diagrams across several buildings — and Table 4.4 reconstructs its path through the office, timestamped from the mailbox records and the estimators' logs.
Inquiry received; sits unread overnight in the shared mailbox
Triaged and assigned to an estimator

Table 4.4. The Innovo inquiry, timestamped from mailbox records and the estimators' logs (M). Touch total: 28 hours. Elapsed: seven calendar days, quote issued two days past the deadline.

Seven calendar days from receipt to quotation; twenty-eight hours of work across three estimators and a weekend of overtime — well above the Tier 3 median of Table 4.2. What made it memorable was not that it was unusual, but that the process could not absorb a job this size inside the deadline, however many people were thrown at it.

It also nearly went wrong, twice. A static head read from the wrong drawing would have undersized the booster set for the taller building — caught only because an odd duty point prompted a second look — and the contractor's reply sat unread for a stretch, because nothing in the process flags a waiting inquiry when its answer arrives. The quotation was late, and it nearly went out wrong, on a marquee project.

Contractor interviews are in progress at the time of writing (protocol in Appendix D): four to six structured conversations covering what drives supplier choice, how speed weighs against price, and — because no live system exists to observe — each contractor's stated reaction to the hypothetical of an automated quote. Preliminary conversations consistently point to response speed and error-free technical submittals as decisive selection factors, which supports the direction of this design; verbatim quotations, including any dissenting views, will be incorporated once transcripts are complete (E, provisional). Stated preferences are the paper's only demand-side evidence, and Section 9.3 treats them accordingly: as an upper bound to be triangulated, not a measurement.

Compressing the evidence of this section — the swimlane timings, the tier metrics, the error audit, and the Innovo inquiry — yields four root causes, shown as a driver tree in Exhibit 4.3. They are worth stating separately because each demands a different remedy, and a design that fixes three while ignoring the fourth forfeits much of the gain.
Exhibit 4.3. Four root causes behind the observed cycle times, quality costs and margin leakage. Each maps to a specific element of the proposed design in Section 7.

Every technical fact the process needs arrives locked inside a PDF, a scan, or a sentence in an email, and is released only by an estimator reading and re-keying it. This is where 1.5 hours of every Tier 2 inquiry goes, and where 41% of defects begin. The Innovo near-miss was this cause in miniature.

One estimator owns an inquiry end to end, so work waits for a person rather than a task, and the scarcest expertise — two people for chilled water — sets the pace for the most valuable inquiries. The 86–88% queue share in Exhibit 4.2 is the signature of serial ownership, not of slow work.

Gaps in the data are discovered mid-process, one at a time, each triggering a round trip to the contractor at a median cost of 41 working hours — and nothing alerts anyone when the answer lands. Thirty-eight percent of inquiries need at least one loop (M); complex inquiries often need two.

Discounts are set without reference points, producing a 4–18% spread on comparable work and the largest single leak in the system. Unlike the other three causes, this one costs nothing in time — only in money, quietly, on jobs that were won.

These four causes are the requirements specification for everything that follows. The intake and extraction layer of Section 7 exists because of the first; confidence-based routing and parallel task design because of the second; automated completeness checks and clarification tracking because of the third; and the rules-based pricing engine because of the fourth. The current state, measured honestly, is the design brief.

This paper draws on four bodies of work, and a fifth that grounds its method. Each is treated instrumentally — a source appears here only because a later section leans on it — and the review's purpose is to establish what is already known so that the paper's contribution stands on settled ground.
5.1 Digitization of B2B distribution and the disintermediation debate

The oldest question this paper raises is whether digitizing a distributor's core function hastens the distributor's own removal. Early electronic-commerce research answered yes: online markets cut transaction costs and let manufacturers deal directly with buyers (Benjamin and Wigand, 1995). The counter-position followed immediately — intermediaries do more than pass product, and new electronic intermediaries appear even as old ones dissolve (Sarkar, Butler and Steinfield, 1995). Chircu and Kauffman (2000) reconciled the two as a cycle of intermediation–disintermediation–reintermediation: displaced incumbents can re-enter by absorbing the technology into the functions that made them valuable, provided they move before a substitute occupies the position. Two decades of wholesale-distribution practice broadly confirms the pattern: distribution consolidated and digitized rather than disappeared, with the gains accruing to distributors that made their differentiating capability digital first.

The relevance is direct: this study proposes to digitize the first of the three pillars identified in Section 2, and the IDR framing turns that from an efficiency question into the strategic one Section 10 resolves — whether automating technical expertise makes the distributor the platform of record for its market, or merely writes the manual for its own replacement. The literature's answer is conditional on sequence, and sequence is a choice.
5.2 CPQ systems and their limits for engineered-to-spec product

Configure-price-quote software is the commercial category closest to this paper's proposal: where a product family can be described by enumerable options and compatibility rules, a configurator reliably replaces expert intervention in the sales process (Forza and Salvador, 2002; 2007) — guided configuration, rule-based pricing and automated quote assembly on top of structured inputs.

The qualifier carries the weight: structured inputs. CPQ assumes the seller already knows, in machine-readable form, what the customer needs; engineered-to-order environments violate that at both ends, with requirements arriving as drawings and specifications rather than option selections, and the mapping to product running through engineering calculation rather than compatibility rules (Hicks, McGovern and Earl, 2000). A pump distributor's RFQ is a textbook instance. That is why Section 6 treats CPQ as a component of the proposed design — the right machinery for pricing discipline and quote assembly — rather than as an alternative to it: what the category has never solved, and what this design must, is the unstructured front door.
5.3 AI document understanding: what the benchmarks do and do not promise

Because this study fields no prototype, published evidence on machine reading of business documents is load-bearing: it supplies the priors the 8.1 audit maps onto the distributor's own document mix, and it must be reported with both its flattering and its unflattering sides. The flattering side is genuine: layout-aware and vision-language models have pushed the standard document-understanding benchmarks to levels out of reach five years ago, with the strongest pipelines answering well above 90% of items on the principal document-QA benchmark (Xu et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2022; Mathew et al., 2021; Jaume et al., 2019).

The unflattering side matters more here. Benchmark corpora are dominated by curated, single-genre documents, while recent enterprise-extraction evaluations show accuracy degrading sharply as schemas widen and documents lengthen — models produce validly structured output whose values are wrong. The distributor's reality sits at the hard end of that spectrum: multi-column schedules scanned as images, specification extracts running to dozens of pages, units and symbols that differ by consultant. And one piece of arithmetic reframes even optimistic per-field accuracy: at 95% per field, a twelve-field schema is fully correct only about 54% of the time (0.95¹²). That arithmetic — not distrust of the models — is why the Section 7 design carries per-field confidence scores, validation gates and human review as structural features rather than as caution, and why the 8.1 audit exists: to establish where on the published spectrum this distributor's documents actually fall.

Four decades of human-factors research warns that the failure mode of partial automation is rarely the machine's error alone; it is the human's changed relationship to the task. Operators over-rely on automation that is usually right and abandon automation that has embarrassed them, in neither case calibrating to its actual reliability (Parasuraman and Riley, 1997). Automation bias — accepting the machine's suggestion in place of one's own vigilance — produces measurable errors even among trained professionals (Goddard, Roudsari and Wyatt, 2012), and strengthens when the human feels less accountable for the outcome (Skitka, Mosier and Burdick, 1999). The design response is to set the level of automation per function, deliberately (Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens, 2000).

The routing design of 7.7 applies these findings directly: confidence is displayed so trust has something to calibrate against; uncertain fields arrive flagged, forcing engagement where it is needed; release is an explicit act with a name attached; and the automation level is set per tier and per function. The literature's uncomfortable implication is retained rather than argued away — a reviewer who approves ninety-nine good drafts is primed to approve the hundredth, and the value-gated release rules and override logging of 7.7 are the design's admission of it.
5.5 Ex-ante evaluation and simulation in operations

This subsection will ground the method of Section 8: the use of business-process simulation to evaluate an operational investment before it is built. It will (i) briefly situate discrete-event and Monte Carlo simulation of service operations in the operations-management literature, (ii) note precedents for simulation-based investment cases, and (iii) introduce the authors' own operations-simulation platform — its modelling approach, calibration method, and validation logic — which is the instrument used in 8.2. Content is pending documentation of the platform's methodology and will be supplied by the authors; two to three citations are expected to be sufficient. Target length: one paragraph.

Five options span the realistic range, from adding headcount to building everything. Each is described on its own terms and scored in 6.2; two of the rejected options survive inside the proposed design as components.

The honest baseline competitor is not technology at all: keep the process of Section 4 and add one or two estimators as volume grows. Its virtues are real — lowest cost, fastest to value, no implementation risk, no change management. Its limits are the arithmetic of 2.2: a qualified estimator costs about €22,000 a year (E), takes two to three months to hire and another three to four to reach full productivity, and adds capacity only in permanent, indivisible steps. Cycle time, error rates and the discount spread stay where Section 4 measured them, because the process itself is unchanged.

Grundfos, Wilo, KSB and Xylem all publish selection software: the estimator enters a computed duty point and picks from the returned range instead of reading curves off the page. This is how most distributors, Khoory included, already work, so its gains are banked in the Section 4 baseline — the tools remove roughly 20 to 30 percent of manual effort at the selection step (E, estimator interviews) and make that step more reliable. They cannot reach intake, extraction, calculation or clarification, where the delay and most of the defects live, and each tool ranks only its publisher's range.

Configure-price-quote software automates the commercial tail: line-item assembly, pricing rules, discount approvals, document generation. As 5.2 established, the category assumes structured inputs and therefore solves the wrong end of this problem — it cannot read a specification, run a head-loss calculation or select a pump — and it addresses only around 10 to 15 percent of the touch time measured in Section 4 (E), at enterprise licence prices. It is rejected as an alternative and retained as a component: the pricing discipline it embodies reappears as the rules-based engine of 7.6.
Option D — full custom AI platform.

Building everything in-house — bespoke extraction models, proprietary hydraulic and selection engines, CAD interpretation from day one — carries the highest capability ceiling and the highest exposure. It duplicates assets the manufacturers already maintain (curve data, selection logic), requires specialist engineering talent the business does not employ, and stakes the schedule on the hardest problems first, against the 5.3 evidence that extraction degrades exactly where this design would need it most. Nothing in the Section 4 baseline requires the ceiling; everything in Section 9 punishes the cost.

QuoteBench assembles proven components under Khoory's own orchestration: foundation-model extraction bought as a commodity, a deterministic in-house calculation engine, the manufacturer selection APIs of Option B repurposed as services, the pricing discipline of Option C rebuilt as rules on Khoory's own data, and confidence-routed human review over all of it (Section 7). Nothing unproven is invented; the claim is in the assembly and the routing. It is the only option that attacks all four root causes of 4.7 at once, and the only one that accumulates a compounding asset while it works — the transaction data of Section 10.

Table 6.1 scores the five options against the six criteria the investment decision turns on, ordinally, from 1 (worst) to 5 (best). The criteria are not equally weighted, and the scores are argued rather than averaged.

Option A wins where a conservative reader looks first: it is the cheapest and the least likely to fail, and an honest matrix says so. What it cannot do is move the operational needles — cycle time, error rate, discount spread — because it adds hands to an unchanged process. D and E dominate the impact criteria and separate on cost and risk: D pays a premium to rebuild what can be bought or borrowed, while E's buy-partner-build sourcing (Table 7.1) confines custom work to thin, auditable layers. B and C score as what they are — useful components mistaken for solutions when deployed alone. The decision therefore reduces to A versus E: certainty and linearity against operational transformation carrying genuine implementation risk. Section 9 prices that trade; 6.3 states the conditions under which A wins it.

What the rejected options do better deserves plain statement. Option A is faster to first value than anything proposed here — an estimator hired in March is quoting by summer, while Phase 1 of Section 11 is still running in shadow — and hiring is reversible in a way build spend is not. The arithmetic has a crossover. At the measured tier mix the average inquiry carries about 4.3 touch hours (M, Table 4.2), roughly €52 of labour at the loaded rate, so below roughly 1,000 pump RFQs a year the touch time a central automation rate could redeploy would not cover the system's amortized build cost (€92,000, one internal engineer-year) and its running costs (developed in 9.4), and hiring would dominate on cost as well as risk (S, register arithmetic; refined in 9.5). The measured single-branch volume of 640 sits below that line: the case for Option E rests explicitly on multi-branch deployment (9.1) and on the benefits hiring cannot buy at any volume — error elimination, discount discipline and response speed (9.2). The commitment is conditional in both directions: if the 8.1 audit returns automation rates materially below its central range, or the pilot of 11.1 breaches its kill criteria, Option A is not this paper's fallback but its recommendation.
Section 7 — Proposed To-Be Process & Solution Architecture

everything in this section is a proposal; nothing has been built. To-be times and behaviours are projections, each carrying the ID of the Appendix A assumption that supplies its value, established by the audit and simulation of Section 8. The proposed system — referred to hereafter as QuoteBench — is governed by five constraints, written as obligations rather than aspirations.

First, automate extraction and calculation; augment judgement — the system takes over the reading, transcription and arithmetic where Section 4.4 located 41% of defects, and presents judgement calls to a person. Second, no quote leaves below defined confidence without human review; in Phase 1 the gate is absolute. Third, every automated decision is auditable — each extracted field, calculation input, ranked option and price logged with source, confidence and timestamp, feeding the liability analysis of 11.3. Fourth, graceful degradation: on any failure, the inquiry drops into the Section 4 manual process with partial work attached. Fifth, every human correction is captured as labelled training data — the constraint that turns review burden into the flywheel of 7.7.
7.2 The to-be process: a projected swimlane

Exhibit 7.1 (Appendix B) mirrors the as-is map lane for lane, with one addition: a System lane into which six of the nine steps migrate, running in minutes. The queues are not compressed but removed — a runtime has no inbox. What remains of elapsed time is one internal queue (the engineer's next free review slot, a projected 2.5-hour median [A6]) and one external wait (the contractor's reply, carried over unchanged from measurement). A projected Tier 2 inquiry would need roughly 25 minutes of human attention against the measured 5.5 hours, the difference redeployed rather than removed (9.2, 11.2).

Within minutes of arrival the intake layer classifies the inquiry into the 4.2 taxonomy [A1] and validates completeness against the 7.4 schema, producing a definitive list of gaps while the inquiry is minutes old. Missing fields trigger one consolidated clarification covering every gap at once [A3] — against an as-is process that finds gaps serially, at a median 41-hour round trip each, and only after roughly 22 working hours of queueing and reading. When the reply arrives, the layer recognises the thread, merges it and resumes, closing the gap that left Innovo's answer sitting unread in a mailbox.

Extraction converts unstructured documents into one canonical record — the twelve-field-per-system RFQ schema of Appendix G — using language and vision models to read specification extracts, schedules and email text. Each field carries a confidence score, and it is these scores, not the values, that drive the routing of 7.7. One boundary is stated now: native CAD parsing is out of scope for Phase 1. Where required fields exist only in a DWG file, the inquiry routes to an engineer with every extractable field pre-filled and the CAD-dependent fields flagged — degradation is to assisted work, not manual — and the 8.1 audit measures how often this occurs.
7.5 The product data layer: classification, storage and retrieval

None of the above works if the system's knowledge of pumps lives inside a language model: models recall approximately, catalogues change monthly, and a quotation defensible under the audit constraint must rest on data that is exact, versioned and sourced. The design therefore separates reasoning from memory. Models read documents and orchestrate; a governed product database remembers — manufacturer data normalized into a typed hierarchy, hydraulic performance stored as curve data rather than prose, prices and lead times versioned with effective dates. The model never answers a product question from its own weights: retrieval runs structured filters first and semantic search second, and any response naming a model must carry the database key and data version it drew from — which is what keeps a quote reconstructible months later and correct the week after a price revision. The full specification of this layer — classification standard, storage architecture, retrieval tooling and ingestion pipeline — is given in Appendix J.
7.6 Calculation and decision layer: three separated engines
Between a validated schema and a draft quote sit three engines, kept separate because they carry different uncertainty. The
hydraulic engine is deterministic physics, not AI

— static head plus friction and fitting losses by Darcy-Weisbach, cross-checked by Hazen-Williams, the same formulas the estimators apply by hand, encoded once; because this is settled engineering, the design's uncertainty lives entirely upstream in extraction, which is what the Section 8 audit measures. The
selection engine is a constrained search

: given a duty point it filters the 7.5 store, queries the manufacturer's selection API, and returns candidates ranked on efficiency, price and lead time, flagging duty points near a curve edge rather than accepting them silently [A5]; where several answers are defensible, Khoory's own history of chosen and winning selections breaks the tie — the Section 10 data asset, used here as a sort order. The
pricing engine is rules, not learning

: cost-plus by family with a defined discount band and a reference price beside every discount decision, aimed at the 4–18% spread and the 1.9%-of-revenue leak of 4.4; machine-learned price optimisation is deferred to Phase 3.
The preceding layers describe what the machine would do; this one decides what it is allowed to do. The routing is stated as logic:
IF   min. field confidence ≥ C₁ AND tier = 1 AND value < €V₁ AND discount in band
THEN auto-draft quote → engineer one-click release
ELIF tier ≤ 2 AND min. field confidence ≥ C₂
THEN engineer workspace: pre-filled schema, flagged uncertainties, ranked options
ELSE full engineer workspace + senior review (Tier 3, CAD-dependent, low confidence)

The thresholds C₁, C₂ and V₁ are design parameters, not findings; setting them is the work of the pilot in 11.1. Under this routing the estimator's role moves upward — exception-handler and advisor, owning the flagged uncertainties, the curve-edge calls and the Tier 3 work that genuinely needs judgement (11.2). Constraint five powers the correction flywheel of Exhibit 7.3 (Appendix B): corrections become labelled data, accuracy rises, routing admits more inquiries to the assisted paths, and freed capacity concentrates where margin is highest — a projected mechanism the pilot exists to observe. Error containment closes the loop: value-gated release regardless of confidence, escalation for out-of-band discounts, an immutable audit log, and a single switch back to manual. Whose signature a quote carries is taken up in 11.3.

7.9 The Innovo inquiry, to-be: a simulated walk-through
What follows is a simulated scenario: the inquiry of Section 4.5 processed under the proposed design, with step times drawn from the Section 8 assumptions. Nothing in it has happened.

Thursday, 16:40: the email lands and intake opens it within the minute — classified, valued, in band [A1]. By 16:52 extraction has populated the schema and validation has found the same gaps a human found on day two, with the riser ambiguity flagged as an explicit conflict [A2]; at 16:53 a single consolidated clarification is on its way, thirteen minutes after receipt instead of 22 working hours [A3]. The contractor's reply is the one interval no redesign controls, so it is carried over at its measured pace: the request is seen on Friday and answered Monday morning. Within minutes of the reply the system has merged the thread, re-validated, run the head-loss calculations, filtered the product store, queried the selection API, and holds a draft quote — models ranked, the booster duty point flagged near its curve edge, prices in band. It is waiting on someone, rather than someone waiting on it. At 14:00 Monday, the estimator's first free slot, the review turns on the flagged selections; the senior's confirmation is two lines, one alternate is added, the discount stays in band [A6, A7]. At 15:10 Monday the quote would go out with the estimator's name on it per 11.3 — a day ahead of the deadline instead of two days late. Seven calendar days would become four; twenty-eight touch hours would become roughly [2.5–3, pending the Section 8 simulation] — the review of a 75-pump draft rather than its manual construction; and neither near-miss of 4.5 would arise to be caught. The conditional tense is deliberate — these times are model outputs — but the contrast is with numbers that were measured, and closing that asymmetry is Section 8's job.

The design would be admitted in stages, each earning the next through a pre-defined gate. Phase 1 runs the pipeline in shadow, every quote human-released and scored against the estimators — Phase 1 is the pilot itself. Phase 2 opens auto-draft for Tier 1 only, gated on live extraction accuracy, override rates and zero escaped defects in shadow. Phase 3 makes assisted routing the Tier 2 default and revisits the deferred items — pricing optimization, CAD — on the strength of accumulated flywheel data. Appendix J (extract) — Product Data Layer: Technical Specification

Manufacturer data is normalized at ingestion into a four-level hierarchy — family, range, model, configuration — with each configuration carrying typed attributes in four groups: hydraulic (performance stored as Q–H, efficiency, power and NPSH point arrays or curve coefficients, never as prose), mechanical (materials, seal type, orientation, connections), electrical (voltage, phase, IE class), and commercial (list price, lead time, supersession chain). Attribute naming follows the ETIM classification standard where the manufacturer supplies it, with a mapping table for house conventions — so that a model designation means exactly one thing to every layer of the system, and remains comparable if further manufacturers are added later.

Two stores, chosen by data type. Parametric and curve data sit in a relational database (PostgreSQL): feasibility questions — which configurations deliver 46 m³/h at 38 m head, in cast iron, at 400 V — are exact filters that must return the same answer every time, and SQL guarantees it. Unstructured technical content — specification sheets, application notes, installation constraints — is chunked, embedded and held in a vector index (pgvector, in the same database) for semantic retrieval when the reviewer or the clarification drafter needs supporting text. Curve data decides this architecture: selection quality depends on interpolating real curves, which is arithmetic on stored coefficients, not language.

The model is granted tools — a structured query against the relational store, semantic search over the vector index, and the manufacturer's live selection API of 7.6 — and its outputs are schema-constrained, so any response naming a model must carry the database key and data version it drew from. Structured filters run first, semantic retrieval second: narrow, then read. Every record carries source and effective date, and each quote references the price-list and curve versions it used. An ingestion pipeline from manufacturer feeds refreshes the store; a record that cannot name its source does not enter it.
